title: How the King of Zoomers Trains to Look like a Greek God (Alex Eubank Program Review)
summary: NH reviews Alex Eubank's 6-day 'Greek God' bro split. He likes the exercise choice and rep ranges but finds it full of junk volume, back-to-back redundant movements, pre-exhaustion and too much shoulder work. He rebuilds it as a 4-day plan and explains why tempo, pump and pre-exhaustion cannot replace load-based progressive overload.
claims: Six training days a week is very hard to justify for novices, who make up most of Eubank's audience
A body-part split is either very good or very bad depending on execution
Eubank's rep ranges (6-12, 10, 12, no 25-30s) suit aesthetics, though a 6-rep minimum never lets you taste 4-8 intensity
Seeing time-tested exercises rather than novelty movements in a program is a good sign
Upper body exercise selection should look like a laundry list, lower body like a Post-it, because lower-body lifts bring more volume and systemic fatigue
Old YouTube programs of bench, squat, deadlift, rows and pull-ups built poor physiques by ignoring many muscles; abs, neck and forearms are still neglected
Chest and back are antagonists, so pairing them avoids competing for performance
Pre-exhausting chest with pec deck before pressing is a mistake; pre-fatiguing lats with straight-arm pulldowns before barbell rows is more defensible because rows use the whole posterior chain
Fixed 12-rep sets mean sandbagging; use a range like 8-12 and let reps drop across sets (12, 12, 11, 10, 8-9)
5 sets of incline DB bench plus pec deck is all the chest work needed for a day; adding flat barbell bench afterward is excess, rotate the two week to week instead
Cable flies after multiple presses are mostly a pump exercise and junk volume; a second pulldown variation the same day is unjustified, rotate instead
Opening shoulders with lateral raises (5x20) then pressing, with three shoulder exercises back to back, is poor programming
Aesthetic lifters hammer shoulders too much, a habit taken from enhanced bodybuilders
Always open with the compound and put isolation after, not before
Eubank's arms lag his very advanced shoulders because his arm days are mostly shoulder work, not because he is natural
Two leg days a week is the bare minimum for anyone beyond a complete novice
Quad-dominant leg days without enough hamstring work can create imbalances that lead to knee issues; pair squats with RDLs and leg curls
Pre-fatiguing hamstrings with leg curls before deadlifts shifts the load to the lower back
Deadlifts for 5x12 are far too much; deadlifts belong at 3-5 reps, use RDLs for higher reps since their stimulus-to-fatigue ratio is better
Squats after deadlifts, leg press and leg extensions are done at maybe 60% and are junk volume
Better split: Mon chest/back/shoulders/triceps, Wed legs/biceps, Thu upper again, Sat legs/biceps; add an arm day later as you advance
Start a program small (3-4 days) and expand; starting at 6 days leaves no room to add
Two sets per body part per day is plenty; slash sets that are not needed
Starting Strength was too intense with too-low reps and ignored muscles; this program is the opposite extreme with too much volume
Programs with that much volume push people to chase the pump just to survive the session
Agrees with Eubank that the best program is one you can stick to and that you should do movements you enjoy
Time under tension cannot replace load: if a muscle can move 50 lb with good form, slowly moving 25 lb is using only 50% of its ability
A 5-seconds-up, 5-seconds-down EZ curl cuts your reps to maybe 20% of normal; add weight and go to failure in a relevant rep range instead
Progressive overload hierarchy: add weight, then reps, then sets, then weekly frequency; drop sets, TUT and pre-exhaustion are only the cherry on top
Warming up a muscle before a compound is fine, but pre-exhaustion lowers its force output, so you get less out of less weight
Enhanced bodybuilders can get away with more volume and less intensity; naturals suffer from it
Without load progression you must keep adding volume to compensate, which is why such programs take hours six days a week
Adding sets at a stuck weight (e.g. a 200 lb bench) eventually just becomes junk volume
At about 170 lb, Eubank is not in his final form and has much room to grow
exercises: pre-fatigues lats; rows use the whole posterior chain so more defensible
mostly a pump exercise after heavy pressing
intense lift; high reps add needless fatigue
trains legs without loading the lower back
